tweets.text: Super Intelligence will begin to exponetially speed up everything SpaceX is doing

thread_tweets.text: Super Intelligence will begin to exponetially speed up everything SpaceX is doing
thread_tweets.full_text: Super Intelligence will begin to exponetially speed up everything SpaceX is doing

thread_tweets.text:
Starship and Raptor design iteration. This is the highest-leverage process at the company. Better models can run more CFD, structural, thermal, and combustion cases, screen geometries, and throw away bad designs before they cut metal. SpaceX already lives on “build, fly, fail, fix.” If you fail more in simulation, the cycle shortens. Faster Starship iteration is what drops the cost of mass to orbit, which then unlocks everything else.

Factory throughput and yield. Designing the next engine is one problem; building thousands of them, plus Starlink and eventually Starmind satellites, is another. Computer vision on welds, tiles, and assembly, plus scheduling and process control, is how you turn a working design into volume. Bastrop, Starbase, and the Raptor lines are the real bottleneck if Elon’s cadence talk is going to happen. Unsexy, and probably more valuable than another 10% better landing algorithm.

Starlink network engineering. Routing, beams, interference, and congestion across a constellation heading toward 100,000 satellites is a classic machine-learning problem. This one already prints money: Starlink did $5.25 billion last quarter at about a 45% operating margin. Squeezing more bits through the same hardware raises capacity and profit without waiting on a new rocket.

Starmind design and operations. Thermal rejection, power scheduling, laser-mesh routing, and where to place workloads across a swarm are greenfield problems, so models can help a lot. This is also the recursive piece: software helping design the orbital computers that then run more software. The payoff is 2028–2029, not next quarter.

Software, firmware, and test generation. SpaceX writes a huge amount of code. Models can draft, review, and generate tests faster, the same way they do at any engineering company. Flight-critical software still has to be verified the old way, so this helps a lot without “exponentially” certifying a rocket.
